t.E110.agn: In its 2009 re-evaluation EFSA lowered the acceptable daily intake (ADI) for this colour and stated that intake in some adults and children may exceed the new limit. EFSA stated that the available data, including the Southampton study, did not confirm a causal link between individual colours and behavioural effects; the EU nevertheless kept the warning label mandatory for products containing it.
t.E110.body: In rats, only a very small proportion (about 3.6%) of orally ingested sunset yellow is absorbed unchanged. The dye is split at the azo bond by gut bacteria; the resulting aromatic amines and aminosulphonic acids (e.g. sulphanilic acid) are partly absorbed and excreted in urine.
t.E110.eff.0.t: May have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children; in the EU this warning is mandatory on the label of products containing it. EFSA did not confirm a causal link with individual colours
t.E110.eff.1.t: The daily limit may be exceeded in some adults and children
t.E110.eval: In the EU, the labels of products containing this colour must carry the warning “may have an adverse effect on attention and activity in children” (following the 2007 Southampton study).
t.E110.prod: An azo dye produced by chemical synthesis.
t.E110.summary: A synthetic, orange-yellow azo dye. It is used in orange-flavoured drinks, confectionery and ready-made desserts.
